title: What Big-O Actually Claims
summary: Big-O is a claim about growth past a crossover point, not a step count. Learn what the notation formally asserts, how O/Θ/Ω differ, and the two misreadings that cost candidates points.

slides.markdown:
Every algorithm question ends the same way: **"and what's the complexity?"** Big-O is the shared language for that answer, and it is the one piece of theory that shows up in literally every coding interview.

Here's what it actually buys you: a way to predict how runtime *changes* when the input grows, without benchmarking anything. You can say a hash lookup beats a list scan at a million items without ever running the code.

What it does **not** give you is a step count or a millisecond estimate. Most Big-O mistakes in interviews come from treating a growth claim as a performance measurement.

slides.subTitle: Past a crossover point, forever after
slides.markdown:
The definition, in plain words: **f(n) is O(g(n)) if there is some constant c and some input size n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀.**

Unpack the two escape hatches, because they are the whole idea:

- **c** lets you ignore constant factors. A function that takes exactly 500n steps is still O(n) — pick c = 500.
- **n₀** lets you ignore small inputs. The claim only has to hold *eventually*. Below n₀, anything goes.

So "binary search is O(log n)" does not say binary search is fast on 10 items. It says: once the array is big enough, the work grows no faster than the logarithm of its size, up to a constant multiple.

That is a **ceiling on growth**, and nothing more.

slides.subTitle: f(n) trapped under c·g(n)
slides.markdown:
Picture two curves on one chart. Your actual cost f(n) wiggles around — it might even sit *above* c·g(n) for small inputs. Then, at some point n₀, c·g(n) crosses over and stays on top forever.

That crossing point is n₀, and everything to the right of it is the region the claim covers. Everything to the left is explicitly excluded.

This is why a merge sort at O(n log n) can genuinely lose to an insertion sort at O(n²) on a 20-element array: at n = 20 you are still to the *left* of the crossover, where the asymptotic claim promises nothing. Real sort implementations exploit exactly this — Python's Timsort and Java's `Arrays.sort` both drop to insertion sort for small runs.

slides.sectionTitle: Why constants and lower-order terms vanish
slides.markdown:
Suppose you count precisely and get **f(n) = 3n² + 200n + 5000**. The Big-O is O(n²). Both the 200n and the 5000 disappear, and so does the 3.

Watch what happens as n grows:

- n = 10 → the n² term is 300, the rest is 7000. The "noise" dominates.
- n = 1,000 → n² term is 3,000,000, the rest is 205,000. Now it's 6% of the total.
- n = 1,000,000 → n² term is 3×10¹², the rest is ~2×10⁸. Under 0.01%.

The fastest-growing term eventually swamps everything else, so the notation keeps only that term and drops its coefficient. That is a deliberate choice: constants depend on your language, CPU, and compiler, while the growth term depends on the **algorithm**. Big-O isolates the part that survives a hardware upgrade.

slides.subTitle: Upper, tight, and lower bounds
slides.markdown:
Three notations, three different claims about the same function:

| Notation | Claim | Everyday reading |
|---|---|---|
| **O(g)** | grows *no faster* than g | upper bound — "at most" |
| **Ω(g)** | grows *at least as fast* as g | lower bound — "at least" |
| **Θ(g)** | both at once | tight bound — "exactly this class" |

Strictly, merge sort is O(n²) — true, but useless, because O is only a ceiling and n² is a very loose one. The useful statement is **Θ(n log n)**: the growth is pinned from both sides.

In interviews, "what's the Big-O?" almost always means "give me the tight bound." Answer with the Θ-style tight class and say the word *tight* — it signals you know the difference. Saying "it's O(n²)" about merge sort is technically correct and will still read as a miss.

A complexity is meaningless until you say what **n** counts. The same function has several defensible answers depending on the variable you pick.

Take "find all pairs of matching words across two documents":

- n = number of words → O(n²) with a naive scan
- n = number of *characters* → the word comparison itself is no longer O(1)
- two inputs of different sizes → the honest answer is **O(a·b)**, not O(n²)

This is why strong candidates open with "let n be the number of nodes and m the number of edges" before analyzing a graph algorithm. Collapsing two independent inputs into one n is the classic graph-question error: BFS is **O(V + E)**, and calling it O(n²) hides the fact that a sparse graph is nearly linear.

State your variables first. It takes five seconds and prevents the whole rest of the analysis from being ambiguous.

slides.sectionTitle: A bound is not a count
slides.subTitle: "O(n) means n operations"
slides.markdown:
The most common misreading: hearing **O(n)** and thinking "this does n operations."

An O(n) function might do 1 operation, or n, or 40n + 12. All three satisfy the definition. The notation caps the *growth rate*, not the work.

Two consequences that trip people up:

- **Two O(n) algorithms can differ by 50x in wall-clock time.** A pass that reads one contiguous array beats a pass that chases pointers through scattered heap nodes, cache miss after cache miss — same Big-O, wildly different reality.
- **An O(1) operation is not necessarily cheap.** A hash lookup is O(1) but computes a hash, probes a bucket, and compares a key. That's dozens of instructions with a constant that a single array index doesn't pay.

"Constant time" means *independent of input size*, not *free*.

The second misreading: assuming a smaller Big-O always means a faster program at *your* input size.

Asymptotic superiority only kicks in past the crossover, and the crossover can be far to the right:

- **Insertion sort beats merge sort** below roughly 10–50 elements. Production sorts hard-code this switch.
- **Linear scan beats a hash map** for tiny collections — no hashing, no allocation, and the array fits in one cache line.
- **Strassen's matrix multiply** is O(n^2.81) versus the naive O(n³), but its constant factor is so large that it only pays off on large matrices.
- **Fibonacci heaps** give better amortized bounds than binary heaps for Dijkstra, and are almost never used, because the constants and pointer chasing eat the win.

The senior move in an interview is to name both: "asymptotically the hash map wins; at n = 20 I'd just scan the array and skip the allocation."

Both of these are Θ(n). One is roughly an order of magnitude slower.

```python
# A: one pass, contiguous memory, no allocation
def sum_array(nums):
    total = 0
    for x in nums:          # sequential reads, cache-friendly
        total += x
    return total

# B: one pass, but allocating and hashing on every element
def sum_via_index(nums):
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        seen[i] = x         # hash, allocate, possibly resize
    return sum(seen.values())
```

Both touch each element exactly once, so both are Θ(n) and both scale identically — double the input, double the time, for either one. But B pays hashing, memory allocation, and dictionary resizing per element.

Big-O correctly says *these scale the same*. It deliberately refuses to say *these are equally fast*. Knowing which question you're answering is the whole skill.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level caveats
slides.markdown:
Complexity analysis assumes a simplified machine, and each assumption is a place where real performance diverges:

- **Every operation costs the same.** It doesn't. An L1 cache hit is ~1 ns; a main-memory miss is ~100 ns. That 100x gap is invisible to Big-O and is why array-based structures routinely outrun "asymptotically equivalent" linked ones.
- **Memory is infinite and uniform.** Real systems page, swap, and GC. An O(n)-space algorithm that exceeds RAM becomes an O(n)-disk-IO algorithm.
- **Only the worst case is quoted.** Quicksort's worst case is O(n²) and it is still the practical default, because that case is vanishingly rare with a randomized pivot.
- **n is the whole story.** Input *shape* — already sorted, all duplicates, adversarial — can move you between cases without changing n at all.

None of this makes Big-O wrong. It makes it a **first-order filter**: it eliminates the algorithms that cannot possibly work at scale, and then you profile.

A complete complexity answer in an interview has four parts, and most candidates give one:

1. **Name the variables.** "n is the number of nodes, m the number of edges."
2. **Give the tight bound, and say which case.** "Worst case Θ(n log n); the average is the same here."
3. **Give space separately.** "O(n) auxiliary, mostly the recursion stack."
4. **Flag the practical caveat if there is one.** "Below ~50 elements I'd just insertion-sort it."

Said together that takes fifteen seconds and reads as fluency rather than recall.

The rest of this group builds each part out: the growth classes you must recognise on sight, how best/worst/average differ, how to derive a bound from source line by line, how recursion changes the technique, and how space and time trade against each other.
